objectives: Students will calculate speed, velocity, and acceleration and explain the difference between speed and velocity.

teach:
Week 8 Science: Physics — Motion, Forces, Newton's Laws, Work, Simple Machines, and Momentum

Objectives

  • Calculate speed, velocity, and acceleration, and explain why velocity needs a direction.
  • Read distance-time and speed-time graphs; find speed or acceleration from them.
  • Find the net force on an object, apply Newton's three laws, and use F = ma.
  • Calculate work and power, and explain how simple machines trade force for distance.
  • Calculate momentum and use conservation of momentum in a simple collision.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors (one for forces, one for motion).
  • Calculator for each student (a TI-30XS or similar, or the on-screen version, is ideal for practice).
  • Printed or on-screen copy of this week's Student Lesson and Study Notes.
  • Index cards for a "Formula Card" (one per student).
  • This week's 12 practice items (course page) for independent practice.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Road-trip speed question; quick vote on which object is "harder to stop."
Direct instruction20Speed, velocity, acceleration; motion graphs; net force and Newton's laws; work, power, simple machines; momentum. Worked Examples 1–5.
Guided practice15The delivery-van scenario: students compute each quantity with teacher support.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (finish for homework if needed).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; students complete their Formula Card; preview the exit ticket and study plan.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Write on the board: "A family drives 150 miles in 3 hours. What was their average speed?" Then ask: "Which is harder to stop: a shopping cart rolling slowly, or a loaded truck rolling at the same slow speed? Why?"

Answers: 150 miles ÷ 3 hours = 50 miles per hour. The loaded truck is harder to stop because it has much more mass, so it has much more momentum at the same speed. Tell students that both ideas, speed and momentum, are formulas they will use today.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. Speed and velocity. Speed tells how fast something moves: speed = distance ÷ time (s = d/t). Units are always a distance unit "per" a time unit: m/s, km/h, mi/h. Velocity is speed with a direction: "20 m/s north." Two cars can have the same speed but different velocities if they travel in different directions. Stress that a car going around a curve at a steady 30 mi/h has a constant speed but a changing velocity, because its direction changes.

Worked Example 1 (speed and velocity). A runner covers 400 meters in 80 seconds while running east along a straight track. Find her average speed and her average velocity.

speed = d ÷ t = 400 m ÷ 80 s = 5 m/s

velocity = 5 m/s east (same number plus the direction)

2. Acceleration. Acceleration is how fast velocity changes: a = (final velocity − starting velocity) ÷ time. Units are m/s2 ("meters per second, every second"). Speeding up, slowing down (negative acceleration, sometimes called deceleration), and changing direction are all accelerations.

3. Motion graphs. Draw two small sets of axes side by side and sketch each shape as you say it. Students confuse these two graphs more than anything else this week.

Shape of lineDistance-time graph means…Speed-time graph means…
Flat (horizontal)Stopped (distance not changing)Constant speed (speed not changing)
Straight, sloping upConstant speed; steeper = fasterSpeeding up at a steady rate
Sloping downMoving back toward the startSlowing down

Key idea: on a distance-time graph, the slope is the speed. On a speed-time graph, the slope is the acceleration.

Worked Example 2 (acceleration from a speed-time graph, then F = ma). A speed-time graph for a 1,000-kg car shows the speed rising in a straight line from 0 m/s at 0 s to 20 m/s at 5 s. Find the acceleration and the net force on the car.

a = (20 m/s − 0 m/s) ÷ 5 s = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s2

F = m × a = 1,000 kg × 4 m/s2 = 4,000 N

Point out the unit: 1 newton (N) = 1 kg·m/s2, so kilograms times m/s2 gives newtons.

4. Forces and net force. A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N). Several forces can act on one object at once. The net force is their combined effect. Forces in the same direction add; forces in opposite directions subtract, and the net force points toward the larger one. If the net force is zero, the forces are balanced and the motion does not change. If it is not zero, the forces are unbalanced and the object accelerates. Weight is a force: weight = mass × g, with g ≈ 9.8 m/s2 on Earth.

Worked Example 3 (net force). A worker pushes a 20-kg crate to the right with 120 N. Friction pushes on the crate to the left with 40 N. Find the net force and the acceleration.

Opposite directions, so subtract: 120 N − 40 N = 80 N to the right

a = F ÷ m = 80 N ÷ 20 kg = 4 m/s2 to the right

5. Newton's three laws.

  • First law (inertia): An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless an unbalanced force acts on it. Example: when a bus brakes, passengers keep moving forward.
  • Second law (F = ma): The acceleration of an object depends on the net force and the mass. More force means more acceleration; more mass means less acceleration for the same force. Rearranged: a = F ÷ m and m = F ÷ a.
  • Third law (action-reaction): When object A pushes on object B, B pushes back on A with an equal force in the opposite direction. Example: a swimmer pushes the water backward; the water pushes the swimmer forward. Emphasize that the two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel each other.

6. Work and power. In physics, work is done only when a force moves an object in the direction of the force: W = F × d, measured in joules (J), where 1 J = 1 N·m. Holding a heavy box still does no work on the box, because the distance is zero. Power is how fast work is done: P = W ÷ t, measured in watts (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. (Point out that "W" means work in the formula but watts as a unit; read carefully.)

Worked Example 4 (work and power). A student lifts a 300-N bag of soil straight up 2 m onto a truck bed in 4 seconds. Find the work done and the power.

W = F × d = 300 N × 2 m = 600 J

P = W ÷ t = 600 J ÷ 4 s = 150 W

If a second student lifts the same bag the same height in 2 seconds, the work is the same (600 J), but the power doubles to 300 W.

7. Simple machines. The six simple machines are the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane (ramp), wedge, and screw. A simple machine does not reduce the work. It changes the size or direction of the force. A machine that lets you push with less force makes you push over a longer distance. Mechanical advantage (MA) = output force ÷ input force. For an ideal machine (no friction), MA also equals input distance ÷ output distance. For a ramp, the ideal MA = ramp length ÷ ramp height. For a lever, the ideal MA = effort arm ÷ load arm. A single fixed pulley has an MA of 1 but changes the direction of the force; a single movable pulley has an ideal MA of 2.

Worked Example 5 (ramp and mechanical advantage). A 900-N piano must be raised 1.5 m onto a stage using a 6-m ramp. Ignoring friction, how much force is needed along the ramp, and what is the mechanical advantage?

Work out = 900 N × 1.5 m = 1,350 J. Ideal machine, so work in = 1,350 J.

Force along ramp = 1,350 J ÷ 6 m = 225 N

MA = 900 N ÷ 225 N = 4 (check: 6 m ÷ 1.5 m = 4)

8. Momentum. Momentum is "mass in motion": p = m × v, measured in kg·m/s. A heavy, slow object and a light, fast object can have the same momentum. In a collision where no outside force acts, total momentum before = total momentum after (conservation of momentum).

Worked Example 6 (momentum and a collision). A 1,500-kg car moving at 10 m/s rear-ends a 1,000-kg car that is stopped. The cars lock together. Find the speed just after the collision.

Momentum before = (1,500 × 10) + (1,000 × 0) = 15,000 kg·m/s

Mass after = 1,500 + 1,000 = 2,500 kg

v = p ÷ m = 15,000 ÷ 2,500 = 6 m/s

Guided Practice (15 minutes) — The Delivery Van

Read aloud and have students work each step in pairs, then share: "A 2,000-kg delivery van starts from rest and speeds up steadily to 12 m/s in 4 seconds. It then drives at 12 m/s for 10 seconds. The driver then unloads a 250-N box by lifting it 0.8 m onto a cart in 2 seconds."

  1. What is the van's acceleration during the first 4 seconds?
  2. What net force acts on the van during the first 4 seconds?
  3. How far does the van travel during the 10 seconds at constant speed?
  4. What is the net force on the van while it moves at a constant 12 m/s?
  5. What is the van's momentum at 12 m/s?
  6. How much work does the driver do lifting the box, and what is his power?

Answers:

  1. a = (12 − 0) ÷ 4 = 3 m/s2
  2. F = 2,000 × 3 = 6,000 N
  3. d = s × t = 12 × 10 = 120 m
  4. 0 N. Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the forces are balanced (first law). The engine's forward push equals friction and air resistance.
  5. p = 2,000 × 12 = 24,000 kg·m/s
  6. W = 250 × 0.8 = 200 J; P = 200 ÷ 2 = 100 W

Checks for Understanding

  • "A line on a graph is flat. What does the object do?" Expected: "It depends on the graph. Distance-time: stopped. Speed-time: constant speed." Students should ask which graph before answering.
  • "A book sits on a table. Gravity pulls it down. Why doesn't it accelerate?" Expected: "The table pushes up with an equal force, so the net force is zero."
  • "Does a ramp reduce the work needed to lift a box?" Expected: "No. It reduces the force, but you push over a longer distance. The work is the same, or a bit more with friction."
  • "Which has more momentum: a 0.2-kg ball at 30 m/s, or a 3-kg ball at 2 m/s?" Expected: 0.2 × 30 = 6 kg·m/s versus 3 × 2 = 6 kg·m/s; they are equal.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Reading the wrong graph. Students see a flat line and say "stopped" on a speed-time graph. Correction: Always read the y-axis label first.

Using one force instead of the net force. In F = ma, F is the net force. Correction: Have students draw arrows for every force, then combine them before using the formula.

Unit mix-ups. Students divide kilometers by minutes and report km/h, or mix grams with kilograms. Correction: Write the units next to every number and convert before calculating (60 minutes = 1 hour; 1,000 g = 1 kg).

Thinking third-law forces cancel. "If the forces are equal and opposite, how does anything move?" Correction: The forces act on different objects. The horse pulls the cart; the cart pulls the horse. Only forces on the same object are added to find its net force.

Believing machines save work. Correction: Repeat "Less force, more distance; the work stays the same."

Differentiation

Support: Give students a formula triangle for each formula (d over s and t; F over m and a; W over F and d). Covering the unknown shows whether to multiply or divide.

Stretch: Ask students to find the distance traveled while speeding up from a speed-time graph (the area under the line; for the van, ½ × 4 s × 12 m/s = 24 m).

How This Shows Up on the GED

Remind students that this week's Practice GED covers the whole science blueprint, not just physics. Physical science is a large part of the GED Science test, and motion and forces are common topics. Expect:

  • Graph questions: "According to the graph, during which time interval was the object at rest?" or "Which statement best describes the motion between 4 and 8 seconds?"
  • Calculation questions in multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank format. The needed formula is usually given in the question or the stimulus (for example, "Momentum is calculated using p = mv"), and an on-screen calculator is available. The skill being tested is choosing the right numbers, doing the arithmetic, and keeping the units straight.
  • Scenario questions that describe an everyday event (a car crash test, a person on a skateboard, a ramp at a loading dock) and ask which of Newton's laws explains it.
  • Drop-down and drag-and-drop items that complete a statement ("The net force on the box is ___, so the box will ___") or sort examples into categories.
student:
Physics: How Things Move and Why

Physics questions on the GED Science test ask you to read graphs, use a short formula, and explain everyday events like braking in a car or pushing a box up a ramp. You do not need advanced math. You need about eight formulas, careful units, and a few big ideas. This lesson gives you all of them.

1. Speed and velocity

speed = distance ÷ time (s = d/t)

Units are a distance "per" a time: meters per second (m/s), kilometers per hour (km/h), or miles per hour (mi/h). Velocity is speed plus a direction, such as "25 m/s west."

Example 1. A bus travels 90 km in 1.5 hours. What is its average speed?

s = 90 km ÷ 1.5 h = 60 km/h

To find time or distance instead, rearrange: d = s × t and t = d ÷ s.

2. Acceleration

acceleration = (final velocity − starting velocity) ÷ time

Acceleration is a change in velocity: speeding up, slowing down, or turning. Its unit is m/s2. A car that goes from 0 to 15 m/s in 5 s has a = (15 − 0) ÷ 5 = 3 m/s2. It gains 3 m/s of speed every second.

3. Reading motion graphs

First, read the label on the y-axis. Then use this table.

Line shapeDistance-time graphSpeed-time graph
FlatStoppedConstant speed
Straight, going upConstant speed (steeper = faster)Speeding up steadily
Going downReturning toward the startSlowing down

On a distance-time graph, speed = change in distance ÷ change in time (the slope). On a speed-time graph, acceleration = change in speed ÷ change in time (the slope).

Example 2. A walker's distance-time graph rises from 0 m at 0 s to 300 m at 200 s, then stays flat at 300 m until 260 s. Describe the motion.

From 0 to 200 s: speed = 300 m ÷ 200 s = 1.5 m/s (constant speed).

From 200 to 260 s: the line is flat, so the walker is stopped for 60 s.

4. Forces and net force

A force is a push or pull, measured in newtons (N). When several forces act on one object, combine them to get the net force:

  • Same direction: add.
  • Opposite directions: subtract. The net force points the way of the bigger force.
  • Net force = 0: forces are balanced. The object stays still or keeps moving at a constant velocity.
  • Net force ≠ 0: forces are unbalanced. The object accelerates.

5. Newton's three laws of motion

LawIn plain wordsEveryday example
First (inertia)Things keep doing what they are doing (staying still or moving straight at a steady speed) unless an unbalanced force acts.You lurch forward when a car stops suddenly.
Second (F = ma)Net force = mass × acceleration. More force, more acceleration. More mass, less acceleration.An empty cart is easier to speed up than a full one.
Third (action-reaction)For every push, there is an equal push back in the opposite direction, on the other object.A skateboarder pushes the ground backward; the ground pushes her forward.

Example 3. A 50-kg skater is pushed forward with 150 N while friction acts backward with 50 N. What is her acceleration?

Net force = 150 N − 50 N = 100 N forward

a = F ÷ m = 100 N ÷ 50 kg = 2 m/s2

6. Work and power

work = force × distance (W = Fd), in joules (J)
power = work ÷ time (P = W/t), in watts (W)

Work is done only when a force moves something in the direction of the force. Carrying nothing, or holding a heavy box perfectly still, does no work on the object. Power tells how fast the work is done.

Example 4. You push a stalled car with a force of 400 N for 15 m. It takes 30 s.

W = 400 N × 15 m = 6,000 J

P = 6,000 J ÷ 30 s = 200 W

7. Simple machines

The six simple machines are the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane (ramp), wedge, and screw. A machine never gives you free work. It lets you use less force over a longer distance (or change the direction of the force).

mechanical advantage (MA) = output force ÷ input force
Ideal ramp: MA = length of ramp ÷ height. Ideal lever: MA = effort arm ÷ load arm.

Example: A 4-m ramp that rises 1 m has an ideal MA of 4. To slide a 400-N box up it (no friction), you need only 400 ÷ 4 = 100 N, but you push for 4 m instead of lifting 1 m. Work is 100 × 4 = 400 J either way.

8. Momentum

momentum = mass × velocity (p = mv), in kg·m/s

Momentum measures how hard it is to stop a moving object. In a collision with no outside forces, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.

Example 5. A 60-kg skater moving at 4 m/s grabs a 40-kg skater who is standing still, and they glide off together.

Momentum before = 60 × 4 + 40 × 0 = 240 kg·m/s

Speed after = 240 ÷ (60 + 40) = 240 ÷ 100 = 2.4 m/s

Formula routine: (1) Write the formula. (2) List each number with its unit. (3) Convert units if needed (minutes to hours, grams to kilograms). (4) Substitute and calculate. (5) Check that the answer has the right unit and makes sense.

Try It

1. A cyclist rides 24 km in 1.5 hours. What is her average speed?

Show answer

s = 24 km ÷ 1.5 h = 16 km/h.

2. A train speeds up from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 8 s. What is its acceleration?

Show answer

a = (30 − 10) ÷ 8 = 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 m/s2.

3. Two dogs pull on a rope toy. One pulls left with 70 N, the other pulls right with 55 N. What is the net force on the toy?

Show answer

Opposite directions, so subtract: 70 − 55 = 15 N to the left. The toy accelerates to the left.

4. A crane lifts a 5,000-N beam 12 m in 20 s. How much work does it do, and what is its power?

Show answer

W = 5,000 × 12 = 60,000 J. P = 60,000 ÷ 20 = 3,000 W.

5. Which has more momentum: a 1,200-kg car at 15 m/s or a 9,000-kg truck at 2 m/s?

Show answer

Car: 1,200 × 15 = 18,000 kg·m/s. Truck: 9,000 × 2 = 18,000 kg·m/s. They have the same momentum.
post:
Post Lesson: Physics — Motion and Forces

Summary of Key Points

  • Speed = distance ÷ time. Velocity is speed with a direction. Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time.
  • Read the y-axis first. Flat line on a distance-time graph = stopped; flat line on a speed-time graph = constant speed.
  • The net force combines all forces on one object. Balanced forces (net force 0) mean no change in motion; unbalanced forces cause acceleration.
  • Newton's laws: (1) inertia; (2) F = ma; (3) equal and opposite forces act on different objects.
  • Work = force × distance (joules). Power = work ÷ time (watts).
  • Simple machines trade force for distance. They do not reduce work. MA = output force ÷ input force.
  • Momentum = mass × velocity. In a collision, total momentum is conserved.

Exit Ticket

1. A delivery drone flies 1,800 m in 120 s. What is its average speed?

Show answer

1,800 ÷ 120 = 15 m/s.

2. What net force is needed to give a 4-kg bowling ball an acceleration of 3 m/s2?

Show answer

F = 4 × 3 = 12 N.

3. A speed-time graph shows a line sloping downward to zero. What is the object doing?

Show answer

Slowing down until it stops (negative acceleration).

4. A person holds a 100-N bag of groceries still for 5 minutes. How much work is done on the bag?

Show answer

0 J. The bag does not move, so the distance is zero and W = F × 0 = 0. (The person's muscles get tired, but no work is done on the bag in the physics sense.)

5. When a cannon fires a ball forward, the cannon rolls backward. Which of Newton's laws explains this?

Show answer

The third law: the cannon pushes the ball forward, and the ball pushes the cannon backward with an equal and opposite force. (This is also an example of conservation of momentum.)

Reflection

  • Which formula do you feel confident using, and which one do you still need to look up? What will help you remember it?
  • Describe one moment from your own week (driving, lifting, sports, work) and name which of Newton's laws it shows.
  • Why do you think car makers design bumpers and air bags to make a collision last a little longer instead of stopping the car instantly?

Test-Taking Strategy: Let the Units Guide You

When a physics question gives you numbers, write each one with its unit. Then look at the unit the answer needs. If the answer is in m/s and you have meters and seconds, you must divide meters by seconds. If the answer is in joules (N·m), you must multiply newtons by meters. Wrong answer choices are often built from the right numbers combined the wrong way (multiplying instead of dividing) or from a skipped unit conversion. Checking units takes ten seconds and catches both mistakes.

vocab.def: How fast an object moves; distance divided by time.
vocab.example: A car that travels 120 miles in 2 hours has an average speed of 60 mi/h.
A plane flying 500 km/h due north.

vocab.def: The rate at which velocity changes: speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. Measured in m/s<sup>2</sup>.
vocab.example: A runner who goes from 0 to 6 m/s in 2 s accelerates at 3 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

vocab.def: A push or a pull on an object, measured in newtons (N).
vocab.example: Friction, gravity, and a hand pushing a door are all forces.

vocab.def: The overall force on an object after all the forces acting on it are combined.
vocab.example: 30 N right and 10 N left give a net force of 20 N right.

vocab.def: Forces that combine to a net force of zero, so the object's motion does not change.
vocab.example: A lamp resting on a table: gravity down equals the table's push up.

vocab.def: The tendency of an object to resist a change in its motion; more mass means more inertia.
vocab.example: A loaded shopping cart is harder to start and stop than an empty one.

vocab.def: A force that acts against motion when two surfaces rub or slide past each other.
vocab.example: Friction between tires and the road lets a car stop.

vocab.def: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg). It does not change from place to place.
vocab.example: A 70-kg person has a mass of 70 kg on Earth or on the Moon.

vocab.def: The force of gravity on an object; weight = mass × g, with g ≈ 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> on Earth.
vocab.example: A 10-kg bag weighs about 98 N on Earth.

vocab.def: Energy transferred when a force moves an object in the direction of the force; W = F × d, in joules (J).
vocab.example: Lifting a 50-N box 2 m does 100 J of work.

vocab.def: How fast work is done; P = W ÷ t, in watts (W).
vocab.example: Doing 600 J of work in 3 s is 200 W of power.

vocab.def: How many times a machine multiplies the input force; output force ÷ input force.
vocab.example: A ramp that lets 100 N of push move a 400-N box has an MA of 4.

vocab.def: Mass in motion; p = m × v, in kg·m/s. Total momentum is conserved in a collision.
vocab.example: A 0.5-kg ball moving at 8 m/s has a momentum of 4 kg·m/s.

Study Notes: Physics — Motion and Forces

Speeds = d ÷ tm/s, km/h, mi/h
Accelerationa = (vfinal − vstart) ÷ tm/s2

Motion Graphs (read the y-axis first!)

  • Distance-time: flat = stopped; straight up-slope = constant speed; steeper = faster; slope = speed.
  • Speed-time: flat = constant speed; up-slope = speeding up; down-slope = slowing down; slope = acceleration.

Net Force

  • Same direction: add. Opposite: subtract (points toward the larger force).
  • Net 0 = balanced = no change in motion.
  • Net ≠ 0 = unbalanced = acceleration.

Newton's Laws

  1. Inertia: no net force, no change in motion.
  2. F = ma: more force, more acceleration; more mass, less acceleration.
  3. Action-reaction: equal and opposite forces on different objects.

Simple Machines

Lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw. Less force, more distance; work stays the same (ideal). Ramp MA = length ÷ height. Lever MA = effort arm ÷ load arm.

Momentum

Total p before = total p after (no outside forces).

Formula routine: write formula → list numbers with units → convert (60 min = 1 h; 1,000 g = 1 kg) → calculate → check units.

stimuli.title: A Cyclist's Commute
stimuli.html: A cyclist rides along a straight bike path from her home to her job. Along the way she stops at a traffic light. The graph shows her distance from home during the 12-minute trip.

stimuli.title: A Test Drive
stimuli.html: Engineers tested a car with a mass of 1,200 kg on a straight, level track. They recorded the car's speed every 2 seconds. The graph shows their results.

stimuli.title: Comparing Moving Objects
stimuli.html:
Momentum (p) is calculated using the formula p = mv, where m is mass and v is velocity. A student recorded the mass and velocity of five objects.

ObjectMass (kg)Velocity (m/s)
Bowling ball6.02.0
Soccer ball0.4020
Toy wagon200.50
Baseball0.1540
Parked bicycle150

items.prompt: During which time interval was the cyclist stopped at the traffic light?
items.hint: On a distance-time graph, what does the line look like when the distance is not changing?
items.explain:
On a distance-time graph, a flat line means the distance is not changing, so the object is stopped. From 4 to 8 minutes, the distance stays at 2 km. The cyclist is stopped.

During 0–4 minutes and 8–12 minutes, the line slopes upward, so her distance from home is increasing. She is moving during those times.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the car's motion from 6 seconds to 10 seconds?
options: The car moves at a constant speed of 18 m/s.
The car is speeding up by 18 m/s every second.
items.hint: Read the y-axis label. This graph shows speed, not distance.
items.explain:
This is a speed-time graph. From 6 s to 10 s, the line is flat at 18 m/s, so the speed is not changing. The car moves at a constant speed of 18 m/s.

"Stopped" is the most common wrong answer. A flat line means stopped only on a distance-time graph. A stopped car would have a speed of 0 m/s, with the line on the x-axis.

items.prompt: During which part of the trip was the cyclist moving fastest?
options: She moved at the same speed for the whole trip.
items.hint: On a distance-time graph, the steeper the line, the faster the motion. Or calculate the speed for each part.
items.explain:
Calculate the speed for each moving part using speed = distance ÷ time:

  • 0 to 4 min: (2 km − 0 km) ÷ 4 min = 0.5 km/min
  • 8 to 12 min: (5 km − 2 km) ÷ 4 min = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75 km/min

0.75 km/min is greater, so she was fastest from 8 to 12 minutes. The line is steepest there. From 4 to 8 minutes she was stopped, and her speed was clearly not the same for the whole trip.

items.prompt: What was the cyclist's average speed, in kilometers per hour, for the entire 12-minute trip, including the stop?
items.hint: Use total distance ÷ total time. Convert 12 minutes to hours first (60 minutes = 1 hour).
items.explain:
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

Total distance = 5 km. Total time = 12 min = 12 ÷ 60 = 0.2 h.

Average speed = 5 km ÷ 0.2 h = 25 km/h.

Common errors: 5 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.42 is in km per minute, not km/h. Leaving out the 4-minute stop (5 km ÷ 8 min = 0.625 km/min = 37.5 km/h) is also wrong, because the question asks about the entire trip.

items.prompt: Acceleration is calculated using the formula a = (final speed − starting speed) ÷ time. What was the car's acceleration from 0 seconds to 6 seconds, in m/s2?
items.hint: Read the speed at 0 s and at 6 s from the graph.
items.explain:
At 0 s the speed is 0 m/s. At 6 s the speed is 18 m/s.

a = (18 m/s − 0 m/s) ÷ 6 s = 18 ÷ 6 = 3 m/s2

Check with any 2-second step on the graph: the speed rises by 6 m/s every 2 s, which is 3 m/s each second. Dividing 18 by 10 (the whole test) is wrong, because the car was not speeding up after 6 s.

items.prompt: Drag each example into the box for the law of motion it best illustrates.
choices: A passenger lurches forward when a bus stops suddenly.
A hockey puck slides across smooth ice in a straight line until it hits the boards.
The same push gives an empty shopping cart a greater acceleration than a full one.
A loaded truck needs a larger net force than a small car to reach the same acceleration.
A rocket pushes exhaust gases downward, and the gases push the rocket upward.
A swimmer pushes backward on the pool wall and moves forward.
items.hint: First law: objects keep doing what they were doing. Second law: force, mass, and acceleration. Third law: a pair of pushes between two objects.
items.explain:
First law (inertia): The passenger keeps moving forward when the bus stops, and the puck keeps sliding in a straight line because nearly nothing acts to stop it until the boards do. Both show objects continuing their motion.

Second law (F = ma): The empty cart has less mass, so the same force gives more acceleration (a = F ÷ m). The truck has more mass, so it needs more force for the same acceleration (F = ma).

Third law: The rocket and gases push on each other in opposite directions; the swimmer and wall push on each other in opposite directions. Each example is a pair of equal and opposite forces on two different objects.

items.prompt:
Two people push on a 10-kg box resting on a smooth floor. Ignore friction. One person pushes to the right with a force of 50 N. The other pushes to the left with a force of 30 N.

The net force on the box is {{0}} toward the {{1}}. Using F = ma, the box's acceleration is {{2}}.

options: neither side, because the forces are balanced

items.hint: The forces point in opposite directions, so subtract. Then use a = F ÷ m.
items.explain:
The forces are in opposite directions, so subtract: 50 N − 30 N = 20 N. The net force points toward the larger force, to the right.

a = F ÷ m = 20 N ÷ 10 kg = 2 m/s2.

Adding the forces (80 N) treats them as if both pushed the same way. 0.5 m/s2 comes from dividing mass by force (10 ÷ 20), and 200 m/s2 comes from multiplying (20 × 10).

items.prompt: A warehouse worker lifts a box that weighs 200 N straight up onto a shelf 1.5 m high. The lift takes 3 seconds. Work is calculated using W = Fd, and power is calculated using P = W/t. What is the worker's power output while lifting the box?
items.hint: Find the work first, then divide by the time.
items.explain:
Step 1, work: W = F × d = 200 N × 1.5 m = 300 J.

Step 2, power: P = W ÷ t = 300 J ÷ 3 s = 100 W.

300 W is the work (300 J) with the time step skipped. 900 W comes from multiplying by the time instead of dividing (300 × 3).

items.prompt: Newton's second law states that F = ma. What was the net force on the 1,200-kg car from 0 seconds to 6 seconds?
items.hint: First find the acceleration from the graph. Then multiply by the mass.
items.explain:
Step 1, acceleration: a = (18 m/s − 0 m/s) ÷ 6 s = 3 m/s2.

Step 2, net force: F = m × a = 1,200 kg × 3 m/s2 = 3,600 N.

400 N comes from dividing the mass by the acceleration (1,200 ÷ 3). 21,600 N uses the speed (18 m/s) instead of the acceleration. 0 N would be correct only for 6 to 10 s, when the speed is constant and the forces on the car are balanced.

items.prompt: A mover needs to raise a crate that weighs 600 N onto a platform 1.0 m high. Instead of lifting it straight up, he pushes it up a ramp that is 4.0 m long. Assuming there is no friction, the work done pushing the crate up the ramp equals the work needed to lift it straight up. What force must the mover apply along the ramp?
items.hint: Work to lift straight up = 600 N × 1.0 m. The same work is done over 4.0 m along the ramp.
items.explain:
Work to lift straight up: W = F × d = 600 N × 1.0 m = 600 J.

The same 600 J is done along the 4.0-m ramp: F × 4.0 m = 600 J, so F = 600 ÷ 4.0 = 150 N.

The ramp's mechanical advantage is 600 N ÷ 150 N = 4 (also 4.0 m ÷ 1.0 m = 4). 600 N ignores the ramp's advantage. 2,400 N multiplies instead of divides; a ramp reduces the force needed, at the cost of a longer distance.

items.prompt: Which two objects in the table have greater momentum than the soccer ball? Select two answers.
items.hint: Find p = m × v for the soccer ball first, then for each choice.
items.explain:
Soccer ball: p = 0.40 × 20 = 8 kg·m/s.

  • Bowling ball: 6.0 × 2.0 = 12 kg·m/s (greater)
  • Toy wagon: 20 × 0.50 = 10 kg·m/s (greater)
  • Baseball: 0.15 × 40 = 6 kg·m/s (less)
  • Parked bicycle: 15 × 0 = 0 kg·m/s (less)

The baseball is the fastest object, and the bicycle has a large mass, but momentum depends on both mass and velocity. An object that is not moving has no momentum.

items.prompt: On a frictionless track, a 2.0-kg cart moving to the right at 3.0 m/s collides with a 1.0-kg cart that is at rest. The two carts lock together and move off as one unit. Total momentum is conserved in the collision. What is the speed of the joined carts just after the collision?
items.hint: Total momentum before = total momentum after. After the collision, the moving mass is 2.0 kg + 1.0 kg.
items.explain:
Momentum before: (2.0 kg × 3.0 m/s) + (1.0 kg × 0 m/s) = 6.0 kg·m/s.

Mass after: 2.0 kg + 1.0 kg = 3.0 kg.

Speed after: v = p ÷ m = 6.0 ÷ 3.0 = 2.0 m/s to the right.

3.0 m/s ignores the added mass of the second cart; the same momentum shared by more mass means a lower speed. 6.0 m/s is the total momentum, not a speed. 1.5 m/s comes from dividing 3.0 m/s by 2.0 kg, which does not use the momentum formula.
